title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
authors: Jiawei Chen, Xiang I. A. Yang, Ping He
abstract: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

infographic.key_insight: DEScover uses four LLM agents to discover physically interpretable DES subgrid length scales from the idea of measuring grid width normal to the local vortex axis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate turbulence-model development while reducing reliance on manual expert formulation.
method: Infer the local vortex axis using alternative vortex-identification methods.
Coordinate four agents to propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate length scales.
Generate CFD simulation scripts to test candidate formulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across flat-plate, backward-facing-step, free-shear-layer, and iced-airfoil tests, the best candidate consistently outperformed the maximum-cell-size baseline and matched or slightly exceeded an expert-designed shear-layer-adapted scale.
infographic.watch_item: The reported average discovery time of about 25 minutes excludes CFD simulations, and generalization beyond the four tested flows remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI

title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
authors: Tom Moussie, Pierric Joseph, Marcello Meldi
abstract: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.

infographic.key_insight: A mixture-of-experts model learns flow corrections from data-assimilated simulations, achieving accuracy close to assimilation without requiring experimental inputs during deployment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to more accurate axial-compressor flow predictions by augmenting baseline RANS with learned forcing terms.
method: Fuse experimental PIV data with steady fixed-grid RANS and unsteady moving-grid hybrid RANS/LES using MFEnKF.
Train neural networks on the enriched database to map local velocity, velocity gradients and turbulent viscosity to forcing terms.
Use a mixture of experts to classify flow regions and combine trained models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against experimental data, the mixture-of-experts predictions show systematically lower discrepancies than baseline RANS and accuracy very similar to MFEnKF.
infographic.watch_item: Individual learned models can produce localized errors near blade tips that exceed baseline RANS errors, making region-aware model selection important.
infographic.paper_title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows

title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: For geometry-aware hemodynamic surrogates, active learning and physical consistency constraints are more effective during fine-tuning than during early or full-training use.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports scalable patient-specific aortic flow prediction while highlighting the importance of training geometries that cover intended clinical anatomies.
method: Generate synthetic aortic CFD solutions with automatically adjusted, physiologically consistent boundary conditions.
Represent anatomies as displacement fields from a common reference and predict peak-systolic velocity and pressure using Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net models.
Evaluate active learning and differentiable finite element residual constraints to improve data efficiency and physical consistency.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports fine-tuning gains from gradient- and subspace-based acquisition and physical consistency objectives, while out-of-distribution tests identify geometric coverage as the primary limitation.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the geometry parametrization's support remains limited; the abstract provides no numerical error or speedup estimates.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows
authors: Yu Jun Loo, Silas Alben, Shravan Veerapaneni
abstract: Matrix-product-state (MPS) and quantized tensor-train (QTT) representations offer a promising framework for computational fluid dynamics, with logarithmic run time and memory scaling in mesh size when bond dimensions remain bounded. Existing MPS-based solvers are Eulerian: they compress velocity fields and enforce immersed-body boundary conditions through static masks or body-fitted coordinates. Moving or flexible bodies complicate this approach: deformation requires updating MPS masks every time step, while filamentary vorticity in high-Reynolds-number flows may resist low-rank compression. We propose a complementary approach: compress the Biot--Savart kernel rather than the flow state, evolve vorticity using Lagrangian vortex particles, and represent immersed bodies by bound vortex sheets on Lagrangian surface points. Our main theoretical result is a lifting theorem: QTT rank $r$ of the kernel implies matrix-product-operator (MPO) rank at most $2^d r$ for the corresponding convolution operator in $d$ dimensions, independent of grid resolution. This bound is sharp for our interleaved ordering. With quantics tensor cross interpolation, the moment-to-local stage of a single-level fast multipole method becomes a precomputed tensor-network contraction with quasi-linear complexity, retaining Lagrangian flexibility for immersed bodies. Our PyTorch implementation (\texttt{DiffVortex}) is end-to-end differentiable, runs on GPUs, and handles $6.7\times10^{7}$ particles on a single device. We validate against reference vortex-method results for an impulsively started cylinder and exact and reference solutions for inviscid elliptical vortices. We also demonstrate two-dimensional flows past rigidly moving, multiple, and deforming bodies, including gradients propagated through the full time integration.

infographic.key_insight: DiffVortex compresses the Biot–Savart kernel rather than the flow state, combining tensor-network acceleration with flexible Lagrangian vortex simulation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its differentiable GPU implementation supports incompressible-flow simulation around moving and deforming bodies, with potential for gradient-based design.
method: Evolve vorticity as Lagrangian particles and model immersed bodies with bound vortex sheets.
Use quantics tensor cross interpolation to precompute tensor-network contractions for fast-multipole moment-to-local interactions.
Prove that kernel QTT rank r yields convolution-operator MPO rank at most 2^d r, independent of grid resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports up to 6.7×10^7 particles on one GPU, validation against cylinder and elliptical-vortex benchmarks, and gradients through full time integration.
infographic.watch_item: Efficiency depends on manageable tensor ranks; the resolution-independent rank bound does not guarantee low ranks for every kernel or configuration.
infographic.paper_title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows

title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics
authors: Wyatt James Horne
abstract: We present Swarmlet, a GPU solver for the unsteady aerodynamics and flight dynamics of one or many multirotor vehicles. The wake is a meshless, evolving-core vortex particle field in the reformulated (rVPM) large-eddy formulation, coupled to rotor models of three fidelities, six-degree-of-freedom vehicles and flight control. Particles carry a smooth core of compact support whose field outside four core radii is exactly the singular Biot-Savart field, so the multipole far field of the treecode carries no regularization error. The subfilter closure is a dynamic eddy viscosity on a fixed filter width, applied by core spreading with a Lagrangian exchange of its local excess under an explicit stability bound, and the strengths are relaxed by projection; global corrections make both the exchange and the relaxation conserve total vorticity and linear impulse. All rotor models shed connected bound circulation, the disks along the arcs swept in each step however long, so the wake receives the lift impulse. The solver agrees with direct summation to $5\times 10^{-7}$ and converges at third order in time. Without calibration, an actuator-line model that includes its own near sheet predicts the hover thrust of a DJI 9443 propeller within 2%. With calibrated section polars it reproduces a Crazyflie propeller's thrust and torque within 3.2% at three speeds and the near wake of a hovering quadrotor with relative $L^2$ differences of 0.08-0.21 against particle image velocimetry, while the wake keeps the delivered impulse. A closed-loop formation of 100 quadrotors, run at a coarser setting on one GPU, illustrates the coupled method at swarm scale.

infographic.key_insight: Swarmlet couples GPU-resident vortex-particle aerodynamics with flight dynamics and control to simulate interacting multirotors while conserving total vorticity and linear impulse.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The solver supports wake-aware analysis of multirotor performance and controlled formations, with a 100-quadrotor demonstration on one GPU.
method: Meshless reformulated vortex particle LES with evolving compact-support cores and an unregularized multipole far field.
Dynamic eddy viscosity via core spreading and conservative exchange, plus conservative strength relaxation.
Three rotor-model fidelities coupled to six-degree-of-freedom vehicles and flight control, with connected circulation shedding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported results include agreement with direct summation to 5×10⁻⁷, third-order time convergence, hover thrust within 2% without calibration, and calibrated thrust/torque within 3.2% with near-wake relative L² differences of 0.08–0.21 against PIV.
infographic.watch_item: The 100-vehicle demonstration uses a coarser setting, so single-GPU swarm feasibility does not establish validation-level wake accuracy at that scale.
infographic.paper_title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics

title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry
authors: Jianxiang Li, Xi Deng, Hong Chul Nam, Anima Anandkumar
abstract: Solving dynamical systems in complex and diverse geometries remains challenging for both numerical solvers and learning-based surrogate models. We propose Neural Operator Splitting, a framework for learning fluid dynamics while preserving the physical structure of fractional-step numerical schemes. Instead of learning the full-step evolution monolithically, we decompose each time step into physically interpretable steps, and learn each operator separately using intermediate states from the underlying numerical solver. Guided by the linearity properties of the fractional steps, we introduce a conditional-linear Fourier neural operator (CL-FNO) whose linear state mappings are modulated by nonlinear conditioning on inputs such as boundary geometry. We further introduce two complementary strategies, symmetry sampling and corrective cycling, to mitigate error accumulation during autoregressive rollout. Experiments on 2D and 3D fluid flows with varying geometries and initial conditions show that our full model reduces mean relative $L^2$ rollout error by 68\% in 2D and 40\% in 3D compared with a single full-step neural operator. At comparable error levels, neural-operator inference is approximately $10^3$ times faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver.

infographic.key_insight: Learning physically interpretable fractional-step operators separately reduces fluid-flow rollout error compared with a single full-step neural operator.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports fast CFD surrogates for varied geometries, with approximately 1,000× faster per-step inference than the Monte Carlo solver at comparable error levels.
method: Decompose each time step and train separate operators using intermediate solver states.
Use conditional-linear Fourier neural operators with linear state mappings conditioned nonlinearly on inputs such as geometry.
Apply symmetry sampling and corrective cycling to limit autoregressive error accumulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on 2D and 3D flows with varying geometries and initial conditions report 68% and 40% lower mean relative L2 rollout error, respectively, versus a single full-step neural operator.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires intermediate solver states; generalization beyond the evaluated geometries and flow conditions remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry

title: Monocular 3D bubble reconstruction: DNS-informed ray tracing and deep learning
authors: Chaitanya S. Nayak, Faizaan Mohammed, Vivek Kumar, Shivam Prajapati, Suhas S. Jain, Cyrus K. Aidun
abstract: Bubble size, depth, and spatial distribution govern transport and uniformity in multiphase flows. A single shadowgraphic view cannot separate bubble diameter from focal-plane displacement, as image signatures depend on both, while multicamera systems add optical access, calibration, and cost. We develop a single-camera physics-guided framework combining direct numerical simulation (DNS), validated Monte Carlo ray tracing, preprocessing, and focus-conditioned multitask deep learning to recover three-dimensional bubble position and physical-equivalent diameter from two-dimensional shadowgraphs. DNS-resolved bubble label images rendered at multiple focal-plane settings. The ray tracer reproduces shadowgraphic signatures with errors below $3\%$ (intensity), $1\%$ (apparent size), $15\%$ (blur), $6\%$ (numerical aperture), and $4\%$ (edge-spread-function shape), running $\sim30\times$ faster than the CPU implementation. The dataset has $900$ frames and $87{,}728$ labeled instances, partitioned by DNS timestamp to prevent leakage and expanded to over $10^{5}$ crops by broad-depth controlled-density rendering. A multitask network predicts signed depth and diameter from crops and focal-plane coordinates, achieving $\sim97.6\%$ normalized depth accuracy on held-out data; a closed-loop DNS-to-image-to-reconstruction test of $180$ bubbles gives diameter error below $9.71\%$ ($\sim90.29\%$ accuracy). On experimental images at four radial planes ($142$--$971$ bubbles each), PDF overlap is $68\%$--$92\%$ and log-PDF correlation is $0.72$--$0.87$. At the focal reference plane ($11{,}679$ bubbles), overlap is $\sim86\%$, correlation is $0.93$, and full-distribution, $D_{99.8}$, and composite errors are below $7.7\%$, increasing with focal-plane distance and defining a recoverability limit. Without stereoscopic hardware, the framework offers a scalable diagnostic for dense bubbly flows.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-guided deep learning estimates 3D bubble position and physical-equivalent diameter from single-camera shadowgraphs without stereoscopic hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a scalable diagnostic for bubble size and spatial distributions that govern transport and uniformity in dense multiphase flows.
method: Render DNS-resolved bubbles with validated Monte Carlo ray tracing at multiple focal settings.
Preprocess bubble crops and train a focal-coordinate-conditioned multitask network to predict signed depth and diameter.
Evaluate on timestamp-separated synthetic data, closed-loop DNS reconstruction, and experimental images.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 900 frames and 87,728 labeled instances, the study reports ~97.6% normalized depth accuracy on held-out data, <9.71% diameter error in a 180-bubble DNS test, and 68–92% experimental diameter-PDF overlap.
infographic.watch_item: Reconstruction errors increase with distance from the focal plane, limiting the depth range over which bubbles can be reliably recovered.
infographic.paper_title: Monocular 3D bubble reconstruction: DNS-informed ray tracing and deep learning

title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver
authors: Pietro Carlo Boldini, Yifu Chen, Marios Kotsonis
abstract: We present DeHNSSo-v2, a major update of DeHNSSo-v1 (Westerbeek et al., Comput. Phys. Commun. 302, 2024), the open-source Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver for nonlinear stability analysis of shear flows. The new release adds a compressible formulation on general two-dimensional body-fitted geometries, automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, reusable per-mode factorizations, and Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions. The curvilinear formulation preserves the fourth-order accuracy of the discretization on strongly distorted grids, and the compressible solver is confirmed to reproduce DeHNSSo-v1 in the incompressible limit. Validation spans published benchmarks for linear instability of compressible flat-plate boundary layers from $\mathrm{Ma}=0.5$ to $\mathrm{Ma}=4.5$, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at $\mathrm{Ma}=1.6$, nonlinear swept-wing crossflow compared with direct numerical simulations, and linear Tollmien-Schlichting wave interaction with a modeled surface-embedded Helmholtz resonator compared with experimentally validated linearized Navier-Stokes simulations. On the nonlinear test cases of DeHNSSo-v1, the computational developments result in a speed-up of approximately one order of magnitude. By broadening the scope and reducing the cost of DeHNSSo-v1, DeHNSSo-v2 provides the boundary-layer-transition and flow-control community with an accessible tool for studying receptivity, nonlinear disturbance evolution, and instability interactions with complex surface geometry and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.

infographic.key_insight: DeHNSSo-v2 extends nonlinear flow-stability analysis to compressible flows and curved geometries while delivering approximately 10× speed-up on DeHNSSo-v1 nonlinear test cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The solver supports boundary-layer transition and flow-control studies involving compressibility, complex surfaces, and metamaterials.
method: Compressible harmonic Navier–Stokes formulation on body-fitted 2D grids with fourth-order spatial accuracy.
Automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, and reusable per-mode factorizations.
Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation includes linear boundary-layer instability benchmarks at Mach 0.5–4.5, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at Mach 1.6, swept-wing comparisons with DNS, and resonator-interaction comparisons with experimentally validated simulations.
infographic.watch_item: The reported speed-up applies to selected nonlinear benchmarks; performance and convergence should be checked for each geometry and harmonic resolution.
infographic.paper_title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver

title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow
authors: Nobutaka Taniguchi, Aiko Yakeno
abstract: The evolution of finite-amplitude disturbances is critical in the prediction of laminar-to-turbulent transition. To analyze the transient growth of disturbances, Pralits et al. (J. Fluid Mechanics, 2015) proposed a weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation (WNLOP) analysis that accounts for the effect of mean-flow distortion on the fundamental wave. The present study formulates a WNLOP analysis via Picard--Chebyshev iteration for compressible parallel flows to predict streak breakdown. The formulation incorporates the non-modal amplification of disturbances and their nonlinear interactions for polychromatic waves, considering all the possible nonlinear interactions starting from a finite set of initial wavenumber components. The nonlinear interaction is tracked as a monotonically increasing set of wavenumber components; specifically, the first-order approximation recovers the linear disturbance equation, the third-order approximation corresponds to the amplitude equation of weakly nonlinear theory, and further iterations systematically approach DNS results in the weakly nonlinear regime. By applying the proposed formulation to a subcritical plane Poiseuille flow at Mach number $\mathrm{M}=0.3$ and Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}=3000$, the proposed formulation demonstrates high predictive accuracy in comparison with DNS calculations and succeeds in identifying the optimal perturbation restricted to a planar wave that causes streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation. The proposed method predicts the nonlinear interaction between the streak and the planar wave, which generates an oblique wave and subsequent harmonic waves characterized by an alternating streamwise vortex structure, whose amplitude determines whether further nonlinear interactions are induced to trigger the turbulent transition.

infographic.key_insight: Picard–Chebyshev weakly nonlinear analysis predicts how streak–planar-wave interactions generate oblique waves and harmonics that can trigger streak breakdown.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting finite-amplitude transition triggers can inform disturbance-sensitive design and flow-control strategies for wall-bounded flows.
method: Formulate weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation analysis for compressible parallel flows using Picard–Chebyshev iteration.
Track non-modal amplification and nonlinear interactions across an expanding set of wave components.
Recover linear dynamics at first order and the weakly nonlinear amplitude equation at third order.
infographic.evidence_signal: For plane Poiseuille flow at Mach 0.3 and Reynolds number 3000, the abstract reports close agreement with DNS and identifies an optimal planar-wave perturbation that triggers streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy is established here in the weakly nonlinear regime; broader operating conditions and computational costs as wave components proliferate require assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow

title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics
authors: Seunghyun Joo
abstract: Discrete adjoint methods give the sensitivities that aerodynamic design and data assimilation require, but they remain hard to obtain for flow solvers that run on graphics processors. This paper presents CuAD, a source-to-source automatic differentiation tool that reads CUDA kernels and writes their tangent and adjoint versions as ordinary CUDA source. Its reverse mode is organised around the GPU thread. It adopts the convention of CUDA kernels that inputs and outputs do not alias, recomputes intermediate values instead of storing them, differentiates pure accumulations without a tape and keeps any remaining tape in a fixed thread-local array. We evaluate CuAD on four kernels from simple flow models and on a two-dimensional Euler solver. All generated derivatives pass dot-product tests to round-off, and the adjoint kernels cost two to six times the primal kernels. On a Biot-Savart summation compiled by one compiler, the CuAD adjoint costs about four times the primal at every size, as does Enzyme when the source declares the absence of aliasing with __restrict__. On the unchanged source Enzyme caches the loop in the device heap and costs 9 to 240 times the primal, while the heap tape of Clad costs 60 to 4400 times the primal and fails beyond 8192 vortices. Exact Jacobians assembled from the generated tangents also matter for accuracy. In single precision, the adjoint gradient of a finite-difference Jacobian reaches errors of 45 to 75 per cent on a stiff Burgers problem and of $5\times10^{-4}$ to $4\times10^{-2}$ on a transonic airfoil, whereas the generated Jacobian keeps them below $5\times10^{-5}$ and $3\times10^{-6}$. The applications include the shape sensitivities of lift and drag of a transonic NACA 0012, for which the residual, the boundary conditions and the wall force are differentiated by CuAD and the adjoint agrees with the tangent to $10^{-13}$.

infographic.key_insight: CuAD transforms CUDA kernels into tangent and adjoint CUDA source, enabling accurate GPU-based sensitivities for aerodynamic design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Generated derivatives support discrete-adjoint lift and drag sensitivities while avoiding the gradient errors seen with finite-difference Jacobians in single precision.
method: Generate tangent and adjoint kernels through source-to-source automatic differentiation.
Organize reverse mode by GPU thread, recomputing intermediates and differentiating pure accumulations without a tape.
Assume non-aliasing inputs and outputs; store any remaining tape in fixed thread-local arrays.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four flow-model kernels and a 2D Euler solver, derivatives passed dot-product tests to round-off, adjoint kernels cost 2–6× the primal, and transonic NACA 0012 adjoint sensitivities agreed with tangents to 10⁻¹³.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment requires respecting the non-aliasing assumption and checking fixed thread-local tape requirements for new kernels.
infographic.paper_title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics

title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall
authors: Marco Galli, Nicolò Scaiola, Ferdinand F. J. Schrijer, Fulvio Scarano
abstract: The spatial evolution of a turbulent boundary layer at $Re_τ= 652$ developing across a finite spanwise oscillating wall is investigated with normalised oscillation period of $T^+ \approx 101$ and amplitude $A^+ \approx 7$, yielding a drag reduction of 32\%. The spatial distribution of skin friction is estimated adopting a recently introduced near-wall data nonlinear regression method based on the arctangent function, which circumvents the requirement of high wall-normal resolution to capture the viscous sublayer. The method viability is assessed against reference DNS data, and the trends of measurement errors from experimental data are well reproduced. The local impact of the control action is examined by evaluating the spatial development of scalar fields of turbulence statistics as well as conditional quadrant analysis to link the onset and recovery transients to turbulence events. The boundary layer response is observed to follow an exponential decay law for the skin friction spatial evolution. The decay length-scale corresponds to $0.6$ boundary layer thicknesses $δ$ for the onset transient and $0.9δ$ for the recovery one. The same exponential fit applied to the Reynolds stresses yields a response within $0.5δ$, with the exception of the shear stress peak, that requires a significantly longer distance.

infographic.key_insight: A finite spanwise-oscillating wall reduced turbulent boundary-layer drag by 32%, with skin-friction onset and recovery decay lengths of 0.6δ and 0.9δ, respectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The measured response lengths can inform the placement and sizing of finite wall-actuation sections for turbulent drag control.
method: Investigate a turbulent boundary layer at Reτ = 652 with wall oscillations at T+ ≈ 101 and A+ ≈ 7.
Estimate local skin friction using arctangent-based nonlinear regression of near-wall data.
Track turbulence statistics and conditional quadrant events through control onset and recovery.
infographic.evidence_signal: The skin-friction estimator was assessed against reference DNS data and reproduced experimental measurement-error trends; most Reynolds-stress responses had exponential decay lengths within 0.5δ, except the slower shear-stress peak.
infographic.watch_item: The reported drag reduction does not establish net energy savings after accounting for wall-actuation power.
infographic.paper_title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall

title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
authors: B. Tripathi, A. E. Fraser, P. W. Terry, E. G. Zweibel, M. J. Pueschel, A. M. Beloborodov
abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

infographic.key_insight: Turbulent cross helicity can grow exponentially in sheared, inhomogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence when shear-driven production exceeds effective losses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This instability may inform modeling of energy transfer and magnetic-field generation in conducting-fluid systems with strong shear.
method: Analytically derive a cross-helical shear instability.
Identify production from a nonzero Reynolds–Maxwell stress gradient.
Test the predicted growth using three-dimensional numerical simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that three-dimensional simulations confirm the analytically predicted exponential growth.
infographic.watch_item: Growth requires a nonzero stress gradient and shear above a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.
infographic.paper_title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence

title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction
authors: Biswanath Barman, Rajendra K. Ray
abstract: Reconstructing flow fields from sparse and noisy measurements becomes particularly challenging when data are completely absent from dynamically critical regions, such as the vortex-formation region of a wake. Conventional interpolation and numerical reconstruction methods generally require sufficient spatial or boundary information, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can also face difficulties when sparse and noisy observations provide little or no supervision in the region of interest. To address this gap, we propose a Fourier-feature-embedded complex-valued physics-informed convolutional residual network (FCV-PICRN) for sparse, gappy, and noisy flow-field reconstruction. The framework integrates Fourier features for oscillatory and multiscale structures, complex-valued representations for coupled amplitude--phase learning, and convolutional residual blocks constrained by the Navier--Stokes equations. The method is first verified using the Taylor--Green vortex at $Re=100$ and then evaluated for the cylinder wake at $Re=100$. Three severe missing-data configurations are imposed in the dynamically sensitive wake: a large hole, a large truncation, and a plus-shaped gap extending in both streamwise and transverse directions. These gaps are further combined with additive Gaussian and multiplicative speckle noise. Despite having no supervised velocity data inside the excluded regions, FCV-PICRN reconstructs velocity, pressure, and vorticity with high structural similarity index (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and remains robust under Gaussian noise up to $20\%$. Finally, for forced two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence with $5\%$ Gaussian noise, FCV-PICRN yields lower reconstruction errors than a conventional PINN. These results demonstrate robust physics-informed reconstruction of severely incomplete and noisy flows across laminar and turbulent regimes.

infographic.key_insight: Combining Fourier features, complex-valued learning, and Navier–Stokes constraints enables flow reconstruction across large unobserved regions despite noisy measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help recover velocity, pressure, and vorticity fields when flow measurements are sparse, noisy, or obstructed.
method: Fourier features represent oscillatory and multiscale flow structures.
Complex-valued representations support coupled amplitude–phase learning.
Convolutional residual blocks enforce Navier–Stokes physics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests cover Taylor–Green and cylinder-wake flows at Re=100, three severe wake-gap geometries, robustness to Gaussian noise up to 20%, and lower errors than a conventional PINN on forced 2D Kolmogorov turbulence with 5% Gaussian noise.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on three-dimensional, higher-Reynolds-number flows and experimental measurements remains unestablished by the reported evaluations.
infographic.paper_title: Fourier-Feature-Embedded Complex-Valued Physics-Informed Convolutional Residual Networks for Sparse and Gappy Noisy Flow-Field Reconstruction

title: Computational and experimental study of multi-grain-size sediment transport and sorting process
authors: Mehrshad Gholami Anjiraki, Gabriel Narh, Jonathan Craig, Mustafa Meriç Aksen, Samin Shapourmiandouab, Ali Farhadzadeh
abstract: Successful prediction of the interaction between turbulent flows and river ecosystems is essential for flood management, development of mitigation strategies, and infrastructure protection. Natural riverbeds consist of bed materials of multiple grain sizes that interact with turbulence differently, leading to spatial classification of particle sizes. Such particle sorting processes can only be captured by models capable of handling multiple grain sizes. We present a numerical framework that couples large-eddy simulation with a multi-grain-size sediment transport module to track multiple grain size classes, their local fractions within the bed-load layer, and bed evolution. A laboratory experiment was conducted in a flume with multi-size bed material to examine sediment particle redistribution and sorting. Measured sediment grain size distributions and bed elevations were used to validate the numerical framework. The results of the multi-grain-size sediment transport model for bed deformation were then compared against those of a uniform sediment transport model, demonstrating that the former reduces the prediction errors relative to the experimental measurements from 37.98 to 3.83 percent for maximum scour depth and from 48.35 to 11.54 percent for maximum deposition height. The validated numerical framework was also applied to large-scale meandering rivers with multi-grain bed material, simulating their bed deformation and sediment sorting. The simulation results revealed the formation of particle sorting patterns in meandering rivers, with coarser and finer sediment particles accumulating near the erosional depression (scour) and depositional (point bar) regions, respectively. These findings support the coupled framework's ability to predict sediment particle sorting and highlight the importance of representing bed material heterogeneity in numerical modeling of meandering rivers.

infographic.key_insight: Coupling large-eddy simulation with multi-grain-size sediment transport improves bed-deformation predictions and captures coarse–fine sediment sorting in meandering rivers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Representing riverbed grain-size heterogeneity can improve scour and deposition assessments for flood management and infrastructure protection.
method: Couple large-eddy simulation with multi-grain-size sediment transport.
Track grain-size classes, local bed-load-layer fractions, and bed evolution.
Validate against flume measurements, then simulate large-scale meandering rivers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Against flume measurements, the multi-grain model reduced maximum scour-depth error from 37.98% to 3.83% and maximum deposition-height error from 48.35% to 11.54% compared with a uniform-sediment model.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports laboratory validation but no field-scale validation of the large-scale meandering-river predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Computational and experimental study of multi-grain-size sediment transport and sorting process

title: Acoustic control of Rayleigh-regime liquid-jet breakup using a through-hole MHz transducer
authors: Kha Nguyen, Kareem Ahmed, James Friend
abstract: This experimental study demonstrates MHz-order acoustic control of Rayleigh-regime liquid-jet breakup using a compact through-hole lithium niobate thickness-mode transducer integrated at the nozzle exit and driven near its 6.7 MHz resonance. Jet dynamics were measured by high-speed shadowgraphy at 50,000 fps, and breakup lengths were obtained from instantaneous jet-length records using an autocorrelation-based method that identifies statistically separated breakup events. Acoustic actuation produced visible interfacial corrugations and reduced the normalized breakup length, $L_b/d$, for both water and glycerol--water jets. In water, the response was threshold-like at low Weber number and weakened as the jet velocity increased to We ~ 50. A reduced-order threshold correlation, fit to the water amplitude and velocity sweeps, captured this abrupt shortening and the subsequent loss of actuation efficacy. More viscous glycerol--water mixtures shortened immediately at low forcing, indicating a distinct acoustic-coupling regime rather than a universal collapse of the water response. A wetting-control experiment showed that liquid spreading at the nozzle base can also shorten the jet, so the measured response reflects coupled radiation-pressure forcing, capillary-wave feedback, and wetting-mediated disturbance injection. Resolved droplet tracking further showed that MHz excitation changes the visible gate-crossing droplet population, although sub-resolution mist and micron-scale atomization were not measured. These results establish through-hole MHz actuation as a compact route for modifying free-surface jet breakup and provide a repeatable image-analysis protocol for experimental-fluid-mechanics measurements.

infographic.key_insight: A compact through-hole MHz transducer shortened Rayleigh-regime liquid jets, with threshold-like behavior in water and a distinct response in more viscous mixtures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Nozzle-integrated acoustic actuation offers a compact way to tune liquid-jet breakup, though effectiveness depends on jet velocity, viscosity, and wetting.
method: Drive a through-hole lithium niobate transducer near its 6.7 MHz resonance.
Measure jet dynamics with 50,000 fps shadowgraphy and autocorrelation-based breakup-event analysis.
Fit a reduced-order threshold correlation to water forcing-amplitude and velocity sweeps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments showed reduced normalized breakup length in water and glycerol–water jets, while the water response weakened as the Weber number approached 50.
infographic.watch_item: Wetting also shortened the jet, complicating attribution to acoustic forcing alone; sub-resolution mist and micron-scale atomization were not measured.
infographic.paper_title: Acoustic control of Rayleigh-regime liquid-jet breakup using a through-hole MHz transducer

title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows
authors: Sinaendhran Pujali Elilarasan, Michael Ullman, Shivam Barwey
abstract: A graph neural network (GNN)-based autoencoder is leveraged to produce reduced latent graph representations of detonation-containing flows. In a two-dimensional hydrogen-air channel configuration with a uniform fuel-air mixture, it was found that latent graphs with effective resolutions of twice the induction length are capable of reconstructing both the wavefront and the post-shock region of the cellular detonation wave structure. Extrapolation studies using stratified and three-dimensional detonation configurations revealed an intrinsic property of GNN-based reconstruction from reduced latent graphs -- a representational hierarchy, rooted in the local nature of message passing, that tends to prioritize features at the detonation front (i.e., the wavefront profile and triple points) over the downstream deflagrative regions. In particular, it was found that at a fixed ambient condition, the information contained in uniform two-dimensional detonations was sufficient to reconstruct the wavefront structure of both stratified and three-dimensional detonations. Overall, this work demonstrates the utility of GNNs for both reduction and information overlap extraction in detonation-containing flows, opening promising pathways for accelerated simulations of these flows.

infographic.key_insight: GNN autoencoders can compress detonation flows into latent graphs while preferentially preserving wavefront features over downstream deflagrative structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact graph representations offer a potential route to accelerated detonation simulations while retaining important wavefront geometry.
method: Encode detonation flow fields into reduced latent graphs using a GNN autoencoder.
Reconstruct cellular detonations in a uniform two-dimensional hydrogen–air channel.
Evaluate extrapolation to stratified and three-dimensional detonation configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Latent graphs with effective resolution twice the induction length reconstructed the wavefront and post-shock region in uniform 2D flows; at fixed ambient conditions, uniform 2D information also supported wavefront reconstruction in stratified and 3D cases.
infographic.watch_item: Local message passing prioritizes wavefronts and triple points, so downstream deflagrative regions may be less faithfully reconstructed during extrapolation.
infographic.paper_title: Reduced graph-based representations of detonation-containing flows

title: Fully resolved particle dynamics over long time scales in acoustofluidic flows: Theory and numerical simulations
authors: Khemraj Gautam Kshetri, Amneet Pal Singh Bhalla, Nitesh Nama
abstract: We present a perturbation-based theoretical framework, together with its immersed boundary/volume penalization implementation, for long-time simulations of fully resolved rigid-particle dynamics in acoustically actuated flows. A perturbation formulation separates the fast acoustic time scale from the slow mean dynamics, avoiding long-time direct integration of the fully compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The immersed rigid body is represented through a Brinkman penalization term in equations posed over a unified fluid-solid domain. The coupled fluid-particle system is decomposed into a time-harmonic first-order problem governing the acoustic response and a time-averaged second-order problem. A central challenge in this decomposition is the treatment of the moving fluid-solid interface. We derive order-consistent expressions for the structural velocities, comprising rigid-body and Stokes-drift contributions, and formulate the corresponding first- and second-order rigid-body equations of motion. For a circular particle in two dimensions, the simulations reveal substantial differences in the magnitude and structure of acoustic streaming around fixed and freely moving particles, highlighting the importance of two-way fluid-structure coupling. The results also show that particle-density effects are more complex than suggested by simplified descriptions based solely on the acoustic contrast factor. The framework captures the mean particle dynamics using time steps associated with the slow particle-motion scale rather than the much smaller acoustic time scale. Finally, simulations of an elliptical particle demonstrate the ability of the method to capture coupled translational and rotational motion. The proposed approach therefore provides an efficient route to fully resolved, long-time simulations of acoustically driven rigid-particle motion while retaining two-way fluid-structure coupling.

infographic.key_insight: Separating fast acoustic oscillations from slow mean motion enables fully resolved, long-time particle simulations while retaining two-way fluid–structure coupling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support acoustofluidic device design by resolving particle translation, rotation, and surrounding streaming without time-stepping every acoustic cycle.
method: Split dynamics into time-harmonic first-order acoustics and time-averaged second-order flow.
Represent rigid particles using immersed-boundary/Brinkman volume penalization.
Derive order-consistent particle velocities and motion equations, including Stokes-drift contributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two-dimensional circular-particle simulations show substantial streaming differences between fixed and freely moving particles and complex density effects; elliptical-particle simulations demonstrate coupled translation and rotation.
infographic.watch_item: Accurate moving-interface treatment is central, and the abstract does not establish quantitative accuracy or speedup beyond the reported demonstrations.
infographic.paper_title: Fully resolved particle dynamics over long time scales in acoustofluidic flows: Theory and numerical simulations

title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
authors: Navneeth Srinivasan, Po-Yu Lai, Suo Yang
abstract: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Combining adaptive tabulation with a neural-network phase-equilibrium model accelerates transcritical multiphase simulations while avoiding iterative-solver convergence failures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a stable, scalable route to high-pressure phase-change simulations relevant to advanced propulsion.
method: Use a pretrained ANN for phase-equilibrium evaluations during ISAT table expansion.
Retrieve tabulated states rapidly through local linear interpolation.
Redistribute tasks with an O(N) greedy load balancer and couple with adaptive mesh refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a Mach 5 shock–droplet benchmark, the framework captured shock–interface dynamics without instability, delivering thermodynamic speedups of 2.30× on one core and 2.62× in parallel over standalone ANNs; AMR added a reported 2.92× overall efficiency boost.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy beyond the demonstrated benchmark requires validation of ANN training coverage and tabulation tolerances.
infographic.paper_title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows

title: Hydrodynamics of microalgae in sea spray
authors: Elettra Figà Talamanca, Juliette Pierre, Eva Ternon, Paula Cohen, Maarten De Rijcke, Hélène de Maleprade
abstract: Airborne transmission of biological matter is likely to cause numerous respiratory distress in coastal populations during certain harmful algal blooms. While we know that dissolved algal toxins aerosolize, the contribution of particle-associated toxins is still unknown. The observation of microalgae in the atmosphere suggests that cells or cell debris could be a carrier. Exchange of particulate matter between ocean and atmosphere is driven by sea spray: microplastics and bacteria aerosolize in jet droplets, following the bursting of air bubbles. However, current models for particle capture only consider surface effects, which fail to explain how large microalgal cells (5-50 um) can be entrapped in jet drops (100-800 um). Here, we demonstrate with a variety of species that microalgae are consistently captured in jet drops, and derive a new particle capture model based on the hydrodynamics of the jet. Using the enrichment factor, which measures the increase in concentration in the first jet drop relative to the bulk, we uncover two regimes. The transition between regimes strongly depends on cell size. In addition, we highlight the dynamics of particles within the jet and derive an enrichment model based on hydrodynamics rather than surface considerations. This work widens and generalizes established results on bacterial and microplastic entrapment in jet drops, resolving discrepancies found in the literature. Finally, we demonstrate that sea spray can aerosolize toxic Ostreopsis cf. ovata cells. This reveals a potential particulate pathway for airborne toxicity during harmful algal blooms and raises the question of the relative contribution of particles to that of dissolved toxins.

infographic.key_insight: Microalgae can be captured in sea-spray jet droplets through jet hydrodynamics, revealing a potential particulate pathway for airborne algal toxins.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hydrodynamic capture models could improve predictions of biological particle transfer from seawater into coastal aerosols.
method: Examine microalgal capture in droplets produced by bursting bubbles across multiple species.
Measure enrichment in the first jet drop relative to the bulk liquid.
Develop a capture model based on particle dynamics within the jet rather than surface effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports consistent microalgal capture, two enrichment regimes with a strongly cell-size-dependent transition, and aerosolization of toxic Ostreopsis cf. ovata cells.
infographic.watch_item: The relative contribution of cell-associated versus dissolved toxins to airborne exposure remains unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Hydrodynamics of microalgae in sea spray

title: Online Seakeeping Forecast Coupling System Identification With Nonlinear Pseudo Spectral Potential-Flow
authors: Zev Hoffman, Sara Vahaji, Micheal Candon, Nirman Jayarathne, Pier Marzocca
abstract: This paper presents a grey-box framework for a robust deterministic, real-time prediction of coupled surge-heave-pitch motion in waves. The approach combines a physics-based online system identification with a nonlinear pseudo-spectral potential flow solver. Rather than prescribing a complete hydrodynamic model from captive model tests or relying on a black-box surrogate, three coupled compact, dynamics equations are identified with constrained ridge-regression of a short time-history of free-running body motion data in waves. The PSPF solver is then used to provide the future incident wave at the body's location. The PSPF and dynamic system models are coupled for continuous real-time future motion prediction in a receding horizon architecture, while the model coefficients are re-identified online to enable robust prediction to changing wave-conditions. This novel framework is demonstrated based on CFD data that has been validated for a freely floating two-dimensional rectangular box in waves. The results demonstrate a feasible framework for accurate motion forecasting up to around eight wavelengths into the future utilising data that can be gathered onboard a ship in real operations. Furthermore, it is shown that the framework is robust to changing sea-states and agnostic to underlying model geometry.

infographic.key_insight: Online system identification coupled with nonlinear pseudo-spectral potential flow enables deterministic forecasts of coupled surge, heave, and pitch up to around eight wavelengths ahead.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support ship motion forecasting using onboard measurements while adapting to changing sea states without a complete pre-calibrated hydrodynamic model.
method: Identify three coupled motion equations from short free-running motion histories using constrained ridge regression.
Use a nonlinear pseudo-spectral potential-flow solver to forecast incident waves at the body's location.
Couple wave and motion models in a receding horizon, re-identifying coefficients online.
infographic.evidence_signal: Demonstration used validated CFD data for a freely floating two-dimensional rectangular box, showing accurate forecasts up to around eight wavelengths ahead and robustness to changing sea states.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on full-scale, three-dimensional ships with noisy onboard measurements remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Online Seakeeping Forecast Coupling System Identification With Nonlinear Pseudo Spectral Potential-Flow
